Kevin Mack Percy Jackson and the Olympians INTERVIEW BY JOE FORDHAM Kevin Scott Mack earned an Oscar for his work on the Impressionistic afterlife imagery in What Dreams May Come, one of many films, including Fight Club, How the Grinch Stole Christmas and Vanilla Sky, that he oversaw as a visual effects supervisor at Digital Domain. After seven years at Digital Domain, he moved on to Sony Pictures Imageworks, producing spectral pyrotechnics for Ghost Rider and candy-colored racecars for Speed Racer. When Mack decided to branch out on his own as a freelance visual effects supervisor, he took on Percy Jackson and the Olympians: The Lightning Thief, the initial entry in a potential film franchise based on a series of children's fantasy novels by Rick Riordan. Mack and his visual effects producer, Denise Davis, oversaw

more than 900 visual effects shots for the production - 811 in the final cut - provided by 13 vendors, including Digital Domain, The Moving Picture Company, Luma Pictures, Pixomondo and Rise Visual Effects Berlin, with added support from Trixter Film, Slash FA, Evil Eye Pictures, Rhythm & Hues, Method, CIS Hollywood and Whiskytree. In the first of several Ancient Greek adventures poised to hit theater screens, the film puts a modern spin on ancient myth, intermingling creatures drawn from Greek mythology - centaurs, satyrs, a gorgon, and the demonic incarnation of Hades, god of the underworld - with disaffected teens and their MP3 players. Artists on three continents furnished the cavalcade of creatures and supernatural happenings that surround Percy Jackson, a teenager who comes to realize his true identity as the 'demigod' offspring of Poseidon, one of Mount Olympus' three most powerful elemental deities. The film's director, Chris Columbus - veteran of the Harry Potter franchise - invited Mack's close collaboration in a rapid-paced production, based in Vancouver. Mack found a kindred spirit in Columbus, who shared his boyish enthusiasm for the material and for the cutting-edge digital technology that would be required to bring it to the screen. Speaking from his Santa Monica home studio - surrounded by his own abstract sculptures, psychedelic glicée prints, and a sizeable collection of electric guitars - Mack reviewed the creative journey of his first freelance supervisory assignment. When you first met with Chris Columbus, how much conceptual work had he done and what was he looking for from visual effects? When I came on board, the production designer, Howard Cummings, was working on set designs, as well as some character designs with conceptual designer Aaron Sims who did the majority of that work. They hadn't done any storyboards at that point. But the most pressing question was whether the movie could be made at all in the time allotted. We had an extremely short schedule, because there were several Greek mythology movies in the works and the studio wanted to get it out there to be the first one in theaters. Chris had proven previously, on Harry Potter, that he was able to work with his editor to cut the film while shooting and turn over sequences early to the visual effects vendors. Once everyone agreed the film could be made in the time frame, Chris started working with several artists, and I got busy with the previz folks. Chris was great to work with in both the creative and the budgeting process. He would weigh what 14П CINEFEX 121 he was willing to let go of, and what he really needed. Did the short preproduction influence the emphasis on what they wanted to do with practical effects, or digital? I'm all for a prosthetic or a practical effect, if it's the right tool for the job. But more often than not nowadays, even if the practical element works, we often don't go that way because digital gives us the flexibility to change it. How did that flexibility come into play in relation to your design work for creatures and effects? Aaron Sims designed a number of creatures - an amazing multi-headed hydra, 'hellhounds' that we see in Hades, a minotaur, Chiron the centaur, and the satyr Grover - and then, a little bit of design work continued when the vendors started building creatures and we saw them in 3D. We sometimes adjusted their proportions, or their color and texture. One of the biggest effects involves Percy discovering that he has the ability to control water, like his father, Poseidon. At the end of the movie, he raises a huge volume of water over New York City. How did that concept evolve? I suggested the idea that Percy was using mentally controllable gravity fields to manipulate water and make it defy gravity. Nobody could grasp what I had in mind. I tried to explain it to an illustrator, and he wasn't getting what I was after. But Chris trusted me. He said, 'I don't get it, but I can tell this is something you feel strongly about, so go ahead and let's pursue it, and we may have to adjust it as we go.' I went away and developed the sequence with visual effects supervisor Kelly Port and his team at Digital Domain. Did you get Digital Domain cooking on that before you shot the plates? I don't know that they began before shooting, because the script was still being worked on. There was a lot of back and forth between visual effects and production. They'd sometimes rewrite the screenplay to match our previz - because what Chris and I came up with for the previz wasn't in the script. We'd come up with ideas, I'd write a little treatment or make drawings, we'd previz that, I'd show it to Chris and he'd make any adjustments he wanted. There's a great tradition of films that use visual effects to combine fantastic imagery and Greek mythology. Ray Harryhausen is synonymous with the genre. Ray was greatly influenced by the art of Gustav Doré, and Doré was playing with thousands of years of tradition. Did you talk about that lineage with Chris, or were you going for something more contemporary? It was very much about making it contemporary. Howard Cummings did all the research about the different gods, what they did, and who was related to whom. Numerous versions of the mythology are contradictory, so he sorted out which versions we would adhere to. Howard was also responsible for giving the live-action production and the sets a realistic look that was a little different than traditional Greek mythology. Mount Olympus, the home of the gods, was not all white pillars and white robes; it was a little darker and grittier, more Gladiator-like. Howard was fantastic to work with, so collaborative and super-talented. He included me in design discussions because they were often intimately linked with visual effects, like when we were doing digital set extensions in Olympus. Did you and Denise Davis sort out the division of labor among visual effects vendors before you started shooting? Some of the work wasn't awarded until we were well into shooting. It was driven, to some extent, by what we believed the facilities could do in the amount of time we had. We took our centaur work and Grover the satyr to MPC because they have done a lot of that on Prince Caspian. They had a clever gag on Caspian where they had characters with backward-bent animal legs running around on Powerizer athletic stilts. Did you ever consider something like that for the Percy Jackson We researched all that stuff, but we had more limited need for those types of effects. We had a centaur race and a few incidental centaurs, but not armies of them charging across fields. Our primary centaur scenes were with Pierce Brosnan, when he appears as Chiron - and we didn't want to put a big movie star on Powerizers. They also tended to produce very bouncy motion that we didn't want for our centaur The other difference from the Narnia films was they went with big, full-sized horse bodies on their centaurs. I wanted to make the horse part smaller, relative to the size of a human. But if we made the horse part too small, it looked like a dog, so we did a lot of back-and-forth previzing those proportions. We wound up with a centaur that had a fairly small horse body, but it was big enough to be ridable, and very muscular. How did Chris film Chiron scenes with Pierce We worked out Chiron's proportions and height, and then special effects supervisor Tony Lazarowich made a pair of drywall stilts for Pierce to wear. To shoot digital leg extension scenes - and this also applies to the centaurs, and Chiron - did you have a survey team on set, witness cameras, tracking markers, lidar? We surveyed all the sets with lidar. We had witness cameras as often as it made sense to. We mostly used a Canon Vixia, a tiny consumer camera that had 24p and high definition. They worked great. We shot wild, no camera sync. We had our own little crew of three to four coordinators and two data wranglers. Sometimes we weren't able to do that if there was more than one camera covering the scene and we couldn't get a good angle, or if we were shooting on two units. Visual effects supervisor Chris Townsend handled second unit for me, and we shared crew and equipment back and forth. Early in the film, we learn that Percy has a reading disability - one of the side effects of being a demigod. How did you visualize Percy's dyslexia? It was tough, because dyslexia is not an optical effect, it's neurological - so how do you communicate that visually? I wanted to avoid letters simply moving and morphing, which is how people who have been afflicted with dyslexia describe the condition. We tried different optical tricks - blurring and refocusing - but we found that anything too fancy wound up being distracting. So we went with a more straightforward 2D effect of letters moving, sometimes with a little jitter, vignetting and shifting focus. MPC, Rhythm & Hues and Slash FX all worked on those effects. Percy sees his first mythological creature in a museum in New York, when one of his teachers turns into a grotesque winged fury. How did you shoot that? Howard Cummings built a set in Vancouver based on the New York Metropolitan Art Museum. Howard, having great insight, helped us out a great deal by giving us rooms with high ceilings. We let him know the dimensions of our fury because she had to leap from a scaffold and fly out through a window, which Howard had to build. For shots of the CG fury grabbing Percy and carrying him around the room, we worked out all the choreography in the previz and then Bobby Brown and the stunt team supplied flying rigs to fly Logan Lerman, who played Percy, around on set. Considering this is a children's movie, how scary did you want the fury to be? We went for broke! It ended up as a cross between an old person and some horrible mutation of a pterodactyl, with three sets of wings. Chris drew a simple, but cool cartoon of how he saw the creature. I took that to Digital Domain, and worked with their concept artist. The actress, Maria Olsen, had very distinctive gums and teeth, so we decided to make that central to our creature. We shot Maria delivering her lines, and used that as reference for the animation. For her transformation, Maria stood up on a scaffold and lurched forward to become the fury. As the fury emerged, we animated her human skin and clothes exploding like a big latex balloon. Digital Domain did a dynamic simulation of that, animating little bits of rubbery skin flying off; then the fury's wings unfolded and it flew down at Percy. Did you shoot any mechanical effects for that? Tony Lazarowich and his special effects team flipped the car. That was all practical, shot out on location. Percy Jackson takes an ascending elevator from the Empire State Building observation deck to a pathway that leads to Mount Olympus, mythical home of the gods of Ancient Greece, which now floats in the clouds above Manhattan in an alternate dimension invisible to mere mortals on the ground. Early on, Chris wanted Poseidon to come out of the ocean and then change scale as he walked down the boardwalk. I was worried that if we showed the character walking and shrinking, it wouldn't read as changing scale; it would look like a zoom out, or like he was going down stairs. We prevized it several ways, and it didn't work. Finally, we had a meeting, and I told Chris and the other folks: 'Look, last night, when no one was looking and it was late and the streets were deserted, I went outside and I grew to 30 feet tall. I practiced shrinking down to normal size, walking and standing still, and I fell down every time. It's impossible to maintain a center of gravity when the bottom of your foot is shrinking, because it's like you're on ice.' They looked at me as if I was out of my mind. That's quite understandable. So what was your I figured since Poseidon is the god of the ocean, when he walked down the boardwalk, he could turn into water. In an instant, a wave runs through him, and he becomes a man made of water. Then, as he walks along, forces blow across him and pull sloshing masses of water back into the sea. He erodes as he walks, shimmying and shifting until he becomes a man-sized blob of water, which then solidifies into a six-foot-tall man. Chris loved the idea, and Luma did a great job with the sequence. We did a similar shot at the end of the film in Olympus. As Percy's walking away from his father, Poseidon turns to water; then we cut to a big splash of water coming towards Percy's back. The water then turns into a hand and grabs Percy's shoulder. It sounds like the production was very open to what visual effects could bring, creatively, to the film - you weren't just connecting the dots. Chris was really good that way. But he was no pushover, either! He had a lot of ideas of his own, and he threw out at least as many of my ideas as he kept. But I encouraged that. I love all the aspects of making shots, from the aesthetics to the very technical, but it's extra fun to be able to contribute creatively at the conceptual level. Curse of the Werewolf ARTICLE BY JOE FORDHAM n 1981, filmmaker John Landis revitalized one of Hollywood's genre icons with the droll but horrific An American Werewolf in London. Few werewolf films since then have had the bonecrunching impact of special makeup artist Rick Baker's Oscar-winning prosthetic and animatronic transformations. Nearly 30 years later, Baker became intrigued at the prospect of returning to his roots when he learned from his friend, makeup artist Dave Elsey - a veteran of Jim Henson's Creature Shop and Star Wars: Episode 3 - that a remake of the Universal Pictures horror classic The Wolf Man was >>>

in the wind. I was at Universal working on the backlot," Rick Baker recalled. "I went into the office of somebody I knew there to see if this was really going to happen. I wanted to be involved because I was such a fan of the original film and werewolves in general. I usually don't pursue jobs like that, but this was too good to pass up. The Wolf Man was important to me. It got me into this business. Re-branded The Wolfman, the screenplay by Andrew Kevin Walker and David Self adhered closely to the 1941 Curt Siodmak story about Lawrence Talbot, estranged son of a Victorian British landowner who, upon returning to his ancestral home after a family tragedy, is bitten and infected by a legendary beast. When Baker approached the production, the film had already attracted director Mark Romanek and actorproducer Benicio Del Toro. Both were keen to employ practical makeup effects for their title character and, while the film was still in development, commissioned Baker for a short design period. Baker enlisted Dave Elsey as his collaborator and eventual creature shop supervisor in England, where the film was destined to be shot. In the eight months prior to the start of production, the two brainstormed designs, mindful of the wolfman's cinematic legacy, which Del Toro wanted to honor. s a starting point, Baker created Photoshop renderings that blended Del Toro's face with aspects of makeup artist Jack Pierce's 1941 makeup on Lon Chaney, Jr. ¿I drew Chaney, Jr. over Benicio's face," said Baker, "then amped that up by throwing in my own ideas. I did an assortment of designs, some much more wolf-like, one that was even more human than Lon Chaney, Jr.' To take the concepts beyond two dimensions, Baker suggested a prosthetic makeup test. Del Toro was shooting elsewhere, and a casting call for potential look-alikes failed to yield a suitable candidate, so Baker sculpted a wolfman muzzle, brow and ears, which he applied as foam latex pieces to his own face and videotaped. "I thought it was a pretty cool test. I sent it to Mark Romanek, and he just said, 'I don't think that's it.' I was disappointed. We were seven months out from shooting and I was hoping for some prep time." The transformations from human to werewolf also remained undefined. When I first met with Mark and Benicio," Baker recalled, "everyone assumed we were going to have a cool transformation, like in American Werewolf. I saw a major problem in that. On American Werewolf, we had a naked man transform into a fourlegged hound from Hell - a completely different anatomy. In this movie, we had Benicio Del Toro, who at 34 • CINEFEX 121 the time had a large beard and a big head of hair that he had grown for Che, so he was already practically a werewolf! I felt that if we started with Benicio, and then had Benicio wearing something like the Jack Pierce makeup on Chaney, Jr., with hair and a minimal appliance, there was no way we'd be able to showcase the transformation by building a change-o-head that stretched out or did all the things we'd done on American Werewolf. I told them I thought it was going to be a really hard nut to crack." *hree months before shooting, visual effects producer Karen Murphy and visual effects supervisor Steve Begg joined discussions to analyze transformation possibilities. Begg shared a desire with Rick Baker to blur the line between digital and practical technology.iWhat first attracted me in a big way to the project," noted Begg, "was the concept of taking Rick's animatronic and prosthetic devices and melding them digitally. I thought that would create quite an unusual look, and certainly people couldn't complain about it looking 'too CGI' because we'd be using real elements." Romanek also explored transformation concepts, at one point inspired by a British television promo of a very slow digital morph from a male to a female performer. Baker suggested a less linear transformation. 'Talbot's body was going through all these painful contortions," said Baker. "I thought it would be interesting if, instead of going from 'A' to 'B,' he went to 'Z' before he went to 'B' - at least it would get a response from the audience." The Tippett Touch ARTICLE BY JODY DUNCAN t the 7th Annual Visual Effects Society Awards ceremony in Los Angeles last year, visual effects icon Phil Tippett was honored with the Georges Méliès Award for pioneering contributions to the art and science of visual effects. Whether by design or happenstance, the award coincided with the 25th anniversary of Tippett Studio, the animation and visual effects powerhouse that had its beginnings in Tippett's garage in 1984. The award presentation started with a short film created by Tippett's longtime friends and colleagues at Industrial Light & Magic, in which Dennis Muren, >>>

Jean Bolte, Pablo Helman, John Knoll and other ILM veterans offered their congratulations and brief commentaries on what Tippett had meant to the film industry. Dennis Muren then appeared at the podium in person, and, after a few remarks, brought a visibly moved Tippett up on stage as the enthusiastic audience rose to its feet and applauded. Tippett then made a speech that was not really a speech at all, but rather a stream-of-consciousness expression of thanks - and some bewilderment at being singled out for the honor.iThere might need to be a little correction here because this thing about 'pioneering,'" Tippett said, "I don't quite get that. In the visual effects racket, the pioneers were those guys who went out when there was nothing and took the 19th century technology and applied it to this new medium of cinema - the Méliès and the Willis O'Briens who, at the turn of the century, really did revolutionize and start our racket. Everything else we've done from that point on has been following in the footsteps of those giants..." Tippett then went on to recall the most traumatizing moment of his career, when Steven Spielberg made the decision that rather than go with classic stop- and go-motion techniques for the dinosaurs in Jurassic Park he would realize them instead with computer animation. 'Steven said: "That's it. That's what we're doing, guys.' It was like: '...I'm doomed! I'm dead...' It was my friends and peers - particularly Dennis, and my buddy and partner Craig Hayes, and my wife Jules - who were able to get me back up on my feet. So much for pioneering. I was dragged kicking and screaming into the digital age. I didn't want to go. It was like going to kindergarten the first time. Some pioneer!" I he humility on display that night was typical of Tippett.iPhil is a very self-deprecating person, commented producer Jon Davison, with whom Tippett has collaborated on several of his most high-profile projects. If someone tries to tell Phil what a wonderful artist he is, he will laugh and reply that if you're still working in the movie business, you are a craftsman. When you're dead, you can be called an artisti Like many visual effects 'craftsmen' of his generation, Tippett had the shaft struck into his heart, as he has described it, when he was seven years old and first saw Ray Harryhausen's 1958 film The 7th Voyage of Sinbad. At that magic moment in a movie theater 52 years ago, Tippett became fascinated by the process of bringing creatures to life through stop-motion animation; and soon afterward, he began sculpting and animating his own figures in clay. ¿I was com60 • CINEFEX 121 pelled as a kid to learn how to do this stuff, because there was nothing there," Tippett commented. "To get exactly what you wanted to work with, you had to make it for yourself. I had no idea how to make balland-socket armatures, of course - that technology was way too complicated for me to figure out as a kid. But I worked in clay or experimented with G.I. Joes and did stop-motion that way, shooting it with an 8mm camera. hil Tippett was born and raised in Berkeley, California, and then, as a teenager, moved to San Diego with his parents in the mid-1960s. One summer day in 1966, he returned home from the beach, turned on the television, and found a man named Bill Stromberg doing a kind of show-and-tell with stop-motion puppets during commercial breaks in the afternoon movie. Stromberg - father to Robert Stromberg, a successful production designer, matte painter and concept artist in the film industry - was a dispatcher for the nearby Carlsbad Police Department who dabbled in stop-motion as an avocation and a hobby. Tippett's father gave Stromberg a call, and the filmmaker soon paid a visit to the Tippett home, bringing with him a 16mm projector so that he could run his stop-motion footage for the enthralled teenager and his family. "After that," said Tippett, "Bill became my mentor, in a sense; and I would go up to Carlsbad to work with him." At the time, Stromberg was animating dinosaur puppets for a production of Ray Bradbury's A Sound of Thunder, a story set in the prehistoric era. We'd shoot stuff and send it off to Rochester, New York, which is where they processed it; and two or three weeks later, we'd get it back. We wouldn't know until then if something was out of focus or if the lighting was off. Stop-motion was this bizarre process of working with no idea of what you were creating. It was kind of like playing piano with earmuffs on, and then listening to a recording of it three weeks later. There was absolutely no feedback.i During this period of working with Stromberg on the Bradbury project, Tippett befriended the prolific author, who urged him to continue with stop-motion and not listen to the naysayers - mainly, his family members - who said he would never make a living in the film industry. Encouraged, Tippett contacted Jim Danforth, an animator who had earned a stellar reputation within the small stop-motion community. Danforth and Dave Allen, another leader in the field, were currently working at Cascade Pictures, creating advertising characters such as the Jolly Green Giant, Mrs. Butterworth and the Pillsbury Doughboy through Seeing Ray Harryhausen's The 7th Voyage of Sinbad at the age of seven sparked in Phil Tippett a fire for bringing characters to cinematic life through the craft of stop-motion animation. Fifty-two years later, Tippett remains at the forefront of the much-changed visual effects industry. This past year, the venerated Tippett Studio - which started in Tippett's garage in 1984 and evolved into a stateof-the-art facility employing a core group of 100 effects artists - celebrated its 25th anniversary. Studio credits garnered in that quarter century include RoboCop, Jurassic Park and Starship Troopers - some of the most innovative and enduring films of the period.

Through the Looking Glass ARTICLE BY JOE FORDHAM rom Time Bandits and The Adventures of Baron Munchausen to his as yet unrealized Don Quixote epic, the themes of fantasy and imagination transcending mortal trappings have long been central to the work of iconoclast filmmaker Terry Gilliam. When a traveling theater troupe's medieval wagon trundled into present-day London in the opening of The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus, it was evident that Gilliam was back on his home turf. The film, scripted by Gilliam and Charles McKeown - screenwriter of Munchausen and Gilliam's Brazil - centers on >>> MOTEL

a Faustian deal between traveling showman Parnassus (Christopher Plummer) and a supernatural being, Mr. Nick (Tom Waits), who has come to claim the soul of Parnassus' beautiful daughter, Valentina (Lily Cole), on her sixteenth birthday. Parnassus barters to save Valentina in exchange for five souls he plans to liberate from their inner fantasies via a magical portal in his 'Imaginarium, aided by his assistants, Percy (Verne Troyer) and Anton (Andrew Garfield), and a charming amnesiac named Tony (Heath Ledger). The project represented a deliberate return to a more personal brand of filmmaking. ¿I wanted to do a compendium," remarked Terry Gilliam. "I was thinking of films like Amarcord, where Fellini had revisited a lot of themes he'd played with in the past. It was the same with Bergman and Fanny and Alexander. I approached Parnassus in that same relaxed and happy spirit." or the first time in years, Gilliam returned to his graphic designer roots and storyboarded Parnassus entirely with his own hand. The renderings became part of a lavishly illustrated art book designed to help win production financing. Other imagery included photographs of Benjamin Pollock's Victorian-style toy theaters from London's Museum of Childhood, and the metaphysical alchemical symbols of 16th-century physician Robert Flood, both used as reference for Parnassus' wagon, together with concept paintings and fine art references. "You've got to give the money people pictures, because they're basically illiterate," Gilliam quipped. "We made several copies of the book to try to get people excited about the potential visuals that we were going to do; but it didn't seem to have any effect on America, because we got our money from Europe and Canada!" Gilliam also made extensive use of 3D previsualizations for the first time in his career, working with previz supervisors Gary Coulter and Caroline Garrett at Fuzzygoat, located at Pinewood Studios, and with Peerless Camera Company, the London visual effects company that Gilliam co-founded in 1976. "In the early script there were far fewer visual effects than we ended up with recalled Peerless visual effects supervisor Paul Docherty, who divided work on the show with independent visual effects supervisor Richard Bain. "There were initially about 250 shots - and that grew, as often happens. Fuzzygoat did some very good previz, largely to work out how much practical set was needed, and partially to work out how we were going to do shots." In the end, it was more practical to divide it up with CG; but I love working with practical models. There's something about being in a real, physical world that always surprises you - the way gravity works, and the way light catches surface textures. All sorts of strange things happen, and you know they're real. We then added CG elements and backgrounds, which is where I think effects work brilliantly, mixing the two media. The production was an emotional and close-knit affair.
